Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations in Sierra Leone record criminal cases and complaints using entirely paper-based methods, such as occurrence books, dockets, and manual files stored in locked cabinets. No evidence of digital case management systems deployed at point-of-service in rural stations; the SLP's 2025-2029 Strategic Development Plan plans an e-Case Management System (baseline survey 2025, implementation 2026+), confirming current paper reliance and need to migrate from paper to digital for criminal records. Key barriers include inadequate electricity especially in rural areas (reliance on thermal generators, poor supply), insufficient internet connectivity in most facilities, lack of computers/printers, and low ICT capacity. Recent digitizations (HR system 2025) and donations (media computers) are urban/regional or non-case related. National ambitions via SLDTP contrast with rural infrastructure gaps, keeping point-of-service recording manual.

revised_comments: Rural police stations in Sierra Leone record criminal cases and complaints entirely on paper, using occurrence books, dockets and manually filed dossiers stored in locked cabinets. The Sierra Leone Police's 2025-2029 Strategic Development Plan sets out plans to move from paper-based records to a digital records management system, including an e-Case Management System, with a baseline survey in 2025 and implementation from 2026, which confirms that paper remains the current default at the point of service. Barriers include inadequate and unreliable electricity, limited internet connectivity, a shortage of computers and printers, and low ICT capacity among station staff, particularly in rural areas. A 2025 initiative to digitise the police's Human Resource processes addresses personnel and payroll administration rather than case or complaint recording. No evidence indicates that rural stations use digital tools for capturing case data at point of service.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Sierra Leone record administrative data such as attendance, enrolment, and learning outcomes predominantly using paper registers and forms. For the Annual School Census (ASC), school heads pre-fill paper questionnaires, which enumerators then digitize using SurveyCTO tablets during visits, verifying on-site headcounts. No evidence found of routine digital tools (e.g., tablets, apps) at rural schools for point-of-service recording; EMIS serves as a national repository for aggregated ASC data, not real-time school-level use.Annual School Census Report 2022Annual School Censuses 2023-2024 In rural areas, QAOs often skip full verification due to remoteness, and connectivity limits uploads; headteachers lack IT skills for digital entry.Sightsavers EMIS Mapping Pilots like SLEAMS (2020, 43 schools) and recent tablet rollouts (e.g., Wi De Ya for attendance, One Tablet per School) exist but are isolated/district-level, not majority rural adoption. Barriers include poor electricity (85% primary schools lack), low connectivity (91% no internet), untrained staff, and infrastructure gaps, especially rural. National ambitions (e.g., NDLS 2025-2030, EMIS strengthening) focus on aggregation/policy, not point-of-service digitalisation in rural facilities, creating a gap where paper remains default.

The Annual School Census is digitised only at enumerator level (via SurveyCTO tablets used by visiting staff), not through routine use by the schools themselves. revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Sierra Leone record attendance, enrolment and administrative data almost entirely on paper registers and forms. For the Annual School Census, school heads complete paper questionnaires which visiting enumerators subsequently digitise using tablets; this digitisation occurs at the point of data collection by external enumerator staff, not through routine digital tools used by the school itself. The Wi De Ya (One Tablet Per School) attendance-monitoring app, which does provide tablets to school leaders for daily digital recording of teacher and pupil attendance, remains limited to around 300 of several thousand government primary schools nationally, with planned expansion to 1,500 and then 4,000 schools not yet procured. Barriers to wider digitisation include poor or absent electricity (most acute in primary schools), very low internet connectivity, and limited digital literacy among headteachers. Paper therefore remains the default method of data capture in the great majority of rural primary schools.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics (PHUs) in Sierra Leone predominantly use paper-based recording for patient data, including forms HF1-HF9 for aggregate service reporting to NHMIS/DHIS2 and paper patient files at point-of-care. A 2022 survey of 55 rural facilities found majority use 1-2 digital tools, mainly DHIS2/eIDSR for aggregate/weekly disease surveillance reporting via tablets/mobile (not individual patient records), with no EMR or patient registries in use; individualized longitudinal data not exchanged.JMIR Formative Research. Digital surveillance rolled out nationwide to 1500+ facilities by 2019, with >95% timeliness/completeness via mobile apps, but limited to epidemiological data.WHO AFRO. Isolated EMR pilots exist (e.g., GOPA-GIZ in 2 rural PHUs in Kambia/Port Loko; planned QEHSSSP hub-spokes in select rural districts), but no nationwide scaling; paper remains default due to infrastructure gaps (power, connectivity).Sierra Leone Digital Health Roadmap 2024-2026. Key barriers: poor electricity/internet in rural areas (50% districts off-grid), hardware shortages, low digital literacy. National ambitions (e.g., DHIS2, strategies) focus on aggregate/surveillance, not point-of-care patient records, creating gap with rural paper reality.

revision_notes: Confirmed. WHO AFRO article (27 June 2025) confirms the eIDSR (DHIS2-based) mobile reporting system operates across 1,500+ facilities for weekly aggregate disease-surveillance reporting, with facility submission rates around 85% following a 2025 maintenance exercise; this is aggregate epidemiological data, not individual patient records. The Sierra Leone National Digital Health Roadmap 2024-2026 notes point-of-care EMR deployment is "on the increase" but describes isolated donor-supported pilots (e.g. GOPA-GIZ in Kambia/Port Loko), not nationwide coverage. The Sierra Leone National Health Compact (World Bank, 2025-2026) sets a target of extending EMR "to all health facilities by 2030", confirming this has not yet been achieved. The original PMC article (PMC9233249) could not be re-fetched (bot-check blocked) but its 2022 finding of limited digital tools used mainly for aggregate/surveillance reporting is corroborated by these more recent sources. Score confirmed at 2 = Mostly paper - some digital.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics (PHUs) in Sierra Leone predominantly record patient care on paper, using forms and paper patient files at the point of care, while digital tools are mainly used for aggregate reporting rather than individual patient records. The nationwide electronic Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (eIDSR) system, a DHIS2-based mobile application, is deployed across more than 1,500 facilities and used for weekly aggregate epidemiological reporting, with facility submission rates around 85% as of mid-2025, but this captures surveillance statistics rather than individual patient histories. Electronic medical record deployment exists only through isolated donor-supported pilots in a small number of districts. The government's National Health Compact and Digital Health Roadmap both set the extension of EMR to all health facilities as a target for 2030, confirming that nationwide point-of-care digitisation has not yet occurred. Constraints include unreliable electricity and internet access in roughly half of districts, hardware shortages, and low digital literacy among health workers, meaning paper remains the primary medium for patient records in rural clinics, supplemented by some digital reporting tools.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural birth registration in Sierra Leone occurs primarily at 1,300 health facilities by 2,600 health workers via MoH memorandum, at chiefdom/community level.UNECA CRVS Snapshot Registration is mostly paper-based; computers only in urban centers, not rural health facilities or chiefdom registries.UNECA CRVS Snapshot NCRA plans expansion but assessments show rural not ready. Digital efforts: national eCRVS upgraded, NIN enrollment ~90%, biometric IDs piloted.ID4Africa PDF 2021 pilot training on mobile app for birth notification in Western Rural health units (outsourced app stores data directly to NCRA).NCRA Training Similar trainings elsewhere, but no evidence of routine point-of-service digital recording in most rural facilities—paper default, digital for aggregate/national.World Bank Blog Barriers: electricity, connectivity, no computers, costs (digital ID 7x paper).The Conversation National ambition (NCRA Act 2016 enables e-systems, 90% coverage) vs rural reality: pilots/donor apps in isolated districts, majority paper at point-of-service (score 2).

revision_notes: Confirmed with updated sourcing. NCRA's Deputy Director of ICT stated at ID4Africa 2025 (reported by Biometric Update, 5 June 2025) that "over 80 percent" of NCRA services are digitised nationally, but also that only around 30% of historic paper records have so far been linked into the digital system, with 70% still requiring digitisation - indicating a substantial ongoing paper legacy. Concurrent 2025 reporting (August-September 2025) shows an MP, community leaders and District Registration Officers publicly lobbying the NCRA Board to decentralise registration services to chiefdom level, stating services remain concentrated at District Headquarters and rural residents must travel long distances to register - indicating that full digital-capture registry offices are not yet present in most rural/chiefdom locations, even though a national digital backend (eCRVS) and mobile registration kits exist for outreach. The original NCRA training source on the Western Rural district mobile-app pilot could not be re-fetched (403 error) but is consistent with a limited-scale pilot rather than routine rural coverage. Score confirmed at 2 = Mostly paper - some digital.
revised_comments: Civil registration in rural Sierra Leone continues to rely substantially on manual, paper-based processes at the point of service, even though the National Civil Registration Authority (NCRA) has digitised much of its central system and reports that over 80% of its services are now digitised nationally as of mid-2025. Around 30% of historic paper records have so far been linked into the digital system, with the remaining 70% still to be digitised, reflecting a large legacy paper base. Registration services and National ID issuance remain concentrated mainly at District Headquarters, and throughout 2025 community leaders, parliamentarians and district registration officers have publicly called on the NCRA to decentralise services to chiefdom level, citing the long distances rural residents must travel to register vital events or obtain identity documents. Mobile registration kits and outreach campaigns, including birth-notification pilots using a simple mobile application at health facilities, extend some digital capture into rural areas, but these remain targeted initiatives rather than standard practice at most rural registry points, where paper forms and manual processes still predominate.
